p: Zhang Jinghui was born on 21 June 1871 in Tai'an, south-west of Mukden in Liaoning Province, an area that became a battlefield in the First Sino-Japanese War. At an early age he joined the Honghuzi irregular cavalry of the Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin, forces that the Japanese recruited as mercenaries during the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905. When Yuan Shikai died in 1916 the Beiyang Army split into mutually hostile factions.

Zhang Jinghui deserted Zhang Zuolin for the Zhili clique of Wu Peifu, but later rejoined him. He served as minister of war in the Beiyang Government from May 1926 to June 1927 and as minister of industry in the National Pacification Army Government from June 1927 to June 1928, and was then appointed governor of the Harbin and China Eastern Railway Special District in northern Manchuria. After Zhang Zuolin was killed in the Huanggutun Incident on 4 June 1928, his relations with the son and successor, Zhang Xueliang, deteriorated.

Following the Mukden Incident and the invasion of Manchuria by the Japanese Kwantung Army in 1931, Zhang called a conference on 27 September to form an emergency committee aiming at the secession of Manchuria from China. He proclaimed his territory self-governing and was inaugurated as governor on 7 January 1932. He then came to terms with Japan and accepted the governorship of Heilongjiang Province in Manchukuo. His refusal to leave Harbin for Qiqihar caused friction with the Kwantung Army, and he was set aside when General Ma Zhanshan accepted the post on 14 February 1932. Ma revolted in April, and Zhang replaced him as minister of defence.

His appointment as prime minister on 21 May 1935 was made at the instigation of the Kwantung Army and over the objections of Emperor Puyi. He is said to have spent his days copying Buddhist sutras and was nicknamed the Tofu Prime Minister in his own lifetime. He is recorded as speaking out against the Japanese administration only once, to criticise the forced sale of land to Japanese colonists. In 1943 he represented Manchukuo at the Greater East Asia Conference in Tokyo; in the same year Time magazine published a false report that he had killed his family and his Japanese adviser and then himself.

After the war the Soviet Union held him in Siberia until 1950, when he was extradited to the People's Republic of China and imprisoned at the Fushun War Criminals Management Centre. He died there of heart failure on 11 January 1959.

notes: The article's second paragraph says 'he was appointed commander of the Beiyang Army's 27th Infantry Brigade' without making clear whether 'he' is Zhang Jinghui or Zhang Zuolin; left out. It also calls Zhang Zuolin 'Viceroy of Three Northeast Provinces' in the last Qing years, which I left out as doubtful.

'He died there' - the article says he was imprisoned at Fushun and 'died of heart failure nine years later in 1959', which implies but does not state that he died in the prison (the existing description says so).
The Time report in the article says he 'poisoned his family and killed his Japanese advisor and other members of the Manchukuo government before committing suicide'; shortened.
